standard.title: Letter formation
standard.description: form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt letter formations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students may have pre-writing experience (drawing, mark-making) but have not yet been explicitly taught and practised standardised letter formations for most of the alphabet.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can form most lower-case and upper-case letters using learnt formations — with a functional pencil grip and consistent starting points, direction and size.

nodes.label: Functional grip and starting point
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use a functional pencil grip and can demonstrate the correct starting point for a modelled letter.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate a functional pencil grip and correctly start at least one letter from the top.
nodes.typical_width: Develop and use a functional pencil grip; follow demonstrations of where to start and in which direction to write letters; apply consistently across practised letters.
wider: Practise grip and formation with different writing tools — pencil, marker, chalk — noting how grip adapts
Use letter formation across different media — sand tray, whiteboard, digital stylus — attending to starting point consistency
nodes.hinge_reason: Incorrect pencil grip and starting-point habits established here directly impair the accuracy and legibility of letter formation in Nodes 2 and 3 — motor habits are increasingly difficult to correct once established.

response_modes.reason: Pencil grip and starting-point habits must be established early and consistently — errors in these mechanics become increasingly hard to correct. Repetition across tools and contexts is the remedy, not breadth.

success_criteria: Student uses a recognisably functional pencil grip.
Student starts letters at the correct point without prompting for practised letters.

nodes.label: Form lower-case letters accurately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can form most lower-case letters using learnt formations — with correct direction and legible shape.
nodes.minimum_width: Form at least fifteen lower-case letters using learnt formations legibly.
nodes.typical_width: Form most lower-case letters using learnt letter formations; demonstrate correct directionality and size; produce legible letterforms in writing tasks.
wider: Apply lower-case letter formations in the context of real writing tasks — labelling drawings, writing names, copying short sentences
Compare letter formation consistency across different surfaces and tools
Explore how printed lower-case letters vary in font and compare with handwritten forms — understanding that the letterform has a consistent structure
nodes.hinge_reason: Lower-case letter formation must be sufficiently established before upper-case letters in Node 3, since upper-case letters are used in conjunction with lower-case in all real writing tasks — inconsistent lower-case production undermines legibility in any written work from this point forward.

response_modes.reason: Letter formation is a motor skill — accuracy and consistency require practice. The width axis is thin here; the issue is reliable production, not contextual breadth.

success_criteria: Student produces most lower-case letters in a recognisable, legible form.
Student's letter formation is consistent across a short piece of writing.

nodes.label: Form upper-case letters accurately
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can form most upper-case letters using learnt formations.
nodes.minimum_width: Form at least ten upper-case letters using learnt formations legibly.
nodes.typical_width: Form most upper-case letters using learnt letter formations; apply in contexts where capitals are required (names, sentence starts).
wider: Use upper-case letters in authentic writing contexts — own name, classmates' names, titles — attending to when capitalisation is required
Compare upper-case and lower-case letter pairs and discuss how formation relates to the letter's identity

response_modes.reason: As with lower-case, upper-case formation is a motor skill requiring practice. Application in authentic contexts (names, titles) reinforces both formation and the rule for when to use capitals.

success_criteria: Student produces most upper-case letters in a recognisable, legible form.
Student uses upper-case letters correctly in their own name.
